title: Reverse-Item Disaster
summary: A six-item fictional scale with two reverse-keyed items that nobody recoded. The learner repairs each reverse item in turn and watches Cronbach's alpha and every item-total correlation move: alpha barely shifts after the first repair, because the second item is still pulling the other way, and only both together give a scale that behaves.
learningObjectives: State the recoding rule for a reverse-keyed item and apply it to an answer.
Explain why an unrecoded reverse item correlates negatively with the rest of a scale.
Read a corrected item-total correlation and say what a negative value means.
Explain why alpha can stay near zero after one of two reverse items is repaired.
Recognise that alpha says something is wrong while the item statistics say which column to fix.
Say why reverse wording is a trade rather than a free correction for agreement bias.
interactionTypes: live scale statistics recomputed from the response matrix on every change
item-total correlation figure, one bar per item, updated after each repair
hand recoding of one answer, applied to that whole item column
two repairs in sequence, with the reliability figure after each
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. Every figure is computed in the browser from the fixed fictional dataset.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout, and the recoding entry accepts Enter. A wrong entry is refused with the rule restated rather than silently corrected. In the item-total figure the sign of each correlation is carried by the direction of its bar and by a printed value, not by colour, and each value is printed on the opposite side of the zero line from its own bar so the two never overlap. The figure carries a description giving alpha and every item correlation in full. Both headline figures are text. No timed content and no motion.
dataStatus: Fictional. All six items are original wording written for this activity, and the six respondents and their answers are invented. No published scale, item or dataset is reproduced, and the reliability figures are arithmetic on invented data rather than results.
simulationNotes: Items are answered 1 to 5 and correct recoding is 6 minus the raw answer, one more than the sum of the scale endpoints. Cronbach's alpha comes from the item variances and the total variance; the corrected item-total correlation is each item against the total of the other five. The six respondents are carried over from the original and the choice matters: perfectly coherent respondents give a less informative pattern. As scored, alpha is -0.04 and four of the six items correlate negatively with the rest, because the total they are measured against is itself broken. With item 3 recoded alpha is +0.03 and only item 5 is still negative, at -0.89. With both recoded alpha is +0.78 and every item is positive. Six respondents is far too few for a real reliability estimate.
readmeTopic: reverse keying, and what an unrecoded item does to a scale's reliability statistics
